questions.title: Value before throughput
questions.stem: A regional insurer wants faster catastrophe claims triage before storm season. Interviews show missing photographs cause most delays; reviewing complete files is already quick. A demonstration classifies complete claims accurately, but incomplete submissions were excluded. The deadline allows one integration. Claims staff retain settlement authority, and management measures time until a file becomes reviewable. Which initial investment BEST follows the evidence?

options.text: Automate settlement-document drafting after approval, retaining missing-evidence collection and measuring total claim turnaround during the pilot.
options.why: This optimizes a downstream stage outside the sponsor's review-ready endpoint.

options.text: Integrate the classifier into the complete-file queue, retaining settlement approval and measuring review-ready time across all incoming claims.
options.why: This preserves authority and measurement, but intervenes after the dominant delay.

options.text: Detect missing required evidence at intake and draft specific follow-up requests, retaining staff approval for customer communications.
options.why: It addresses the observed bottleneck without changing settlement authority.

options.text: Use classification to prioritize incomplete files for manual investigation, preserving existing follow-up messaging and settlement approval rules.
options.why: Triage may redistribute attention, but does not directly improve the identified evidence-collection step.

questions.decision: Choose the measured process bottleneck and business endpoint before optimizing the demonstrated model component.

questions.title: Closing an offline feedback gap
questions.stem: A municipal permit assistant produces draft deficiency notices. Clerks revise drafts in a separate desktop editor, while the AI service records only generated notices and API latency. After launch, repeat submissions increase despite favorable clerk satisfaction. The city needs to trace whether ambiguous notices cause rework without retaining unnecessary applicant data. Which TWO architecture changes most directly support that investigation?

options.text: Send every draft and applicant attachment to a central analytics archive with indefinite retention for later analysis.
options.why: Indefinite sensitive-content capture exceeds the investigation's needs.

options.text: Add a larger language model that predicts clerk satisfaction before a notice leaves the drafting service.
options.why: Predicted satisfaction does not establish the source of rework.

options.text: Capture structured revision reasons and pseudonymous permit identifiers linking the approved notice to subsequent deficiency outcomes.
options.why: This links interventions to outcomes while limiting applicant content.

options.text: Count notices drafted per employee and correlate that weekly total with the citywide resubmission percentage.
options.why: Aggregate throughput obscures which notice caused which outcome.

options.text: Version notice templates and retrieval sources, and assign an owner to test repairs on recurring rework cases.
options.why: This enables reproducible diagnosis and controlled improvement.

questions.decision: Link the approved intervention, its configuration and downstream outcome; give the loop an accountable improvement owner.

questions.title: Conditional branches with known boundaries
questions.stem: A supplier-onboarding process verifies four mandatory documents, checks an authoritative sanctions service, and requests clarification when a field is missing. Every branch and escalation condition is documented; an unresolved match must reach compliance staff. The vendor proposes an autonomous investigator because cases contain free text. The team prioritizes predictable completion and reproducible audit paths. Which implementation is the BEST starting architecture?

options.text: Use a bounded planning agent with the same mandatory checks and compliance escalation, letting it select verification order for each case.
options.why: It can comply, but adds unnecessary dynamic planning to known branches when predictability is prioritized.

options.text: Run four document-review agents and a central compliance approver, exchanging natural-language completion reports before onboarding approval.
options.why: It preserves authority but adds loosely defined handoffs instead of reproducible enforced transitions.

options.text: Use a single augmented-model call that returns structured findings for staff to execute through a separate manual verification checklist.
options.why: It preserves escalation but shifts enforceable routine verification back to staff despite documented automation branches.

options.text: Use a stateful workflow with model-assisted extraction, deterministic branch guards and a compliance escalation state for unresolved matches.
options.why: Known branches favor explicit control while extraction benefits from language understanding.

questions.decision: Free text does not make control flow unknown; encode known requirements around the model-assisted steps.

questions.title: Parallel reviews with a shared release
questions.stem: A media company asks three agents to review an advertisement for brand, factual and regulatory concerns. Reviews are independent, but the agents currently edit one shared draft and sometimes undo each other's changes. Only an editor can approve publication. The company wants parallel speed without losing objections or creating inconsistent drafts. Which TWO design changes BEST preserve those requirements?

options.text: Run reviewers sequentially over one shared draft, retaining editor approval and a revision history for every specialist edit.
options.why: It is safe but gives up the requested parallel review speed.

options.text: Give reviewers immutable draft versions and structured passage-linked findings, preserving the applicable review criterion for each objection.
options.why: Independent analysis avoids conflicting edits while preserving evidence.

options.text: Run reviewers in parallel on separate drafts and send only their final rewritten text to the editor without finding-level provenance.
options.why: The editor cannot reliably distinguish overwritten objections from compatible edits.

options.text: Use one reconciliation step to prepare a coherent proposed revision and unresolved issues for the editor's approval.
options.why: Synthesis preserves a single draft and the required authority.

options.text: Run independent parallel reviews and concatenate every proposed rewrite into the publication draft before the editor approves it.
options.why: Concatenation does not reconcile mutually inconsistent revisions.

questions.decision: Separate independent analysis from shared-state mutation and final authority; parallelism need not mean multiple writers.

questions.title: Dependency-aware decomposition
questions.stem: A construction estimator asks an AI system to divide a bid into independent work packages. Electrical cost depends on the mechanical equipment schedule, and both depend on the approved floor plan. The first prototype runs all estimators concurrently using different document revisions; totals are individually plausible but incompatible. The client wants a reusable decomposition that supports some concurrency. What should the architect change FIRST?

options.text: Define a versioned input contract and dependency graph, completing prerequisite schedules before parallel estimation of independent downstream packages.
options.why: This resolves inconsistent prerequisites while retaining useful concurrency.

options.text: Add a final model that averages conflicting assumptions across all independently generated package estimates before producing the total.
options.why: Averaging does not reconcile incompatible physical assumptions.

options.text: Increase each estimator's context window so every package can independently infer the current approved design from all documents.
options.why: Independent inference still leaves conflicting versions and dependencies.

options.text: Use a majority vote across three complete bid-generating agents, treating the winning total as the consistency check.
options.why: Agreement on totals does not validate package compatibility.

questions.decision: Decompose around stable contracts and causal dependencies rather than merely dividing documents into similar-sized pieces.

questions.title: Adoption-adjusted first-month contribution
questions.stem: A procurement pilot handles 2,400 requests monthly. On adopted requests it saves six minutes of staff handling, valued at $40 per hour under an approved redeployment plan. Adoption is 75%. Each adopted request also incurs $0.80 of expected review/rework cost. A $250 monthly service fee and a one-time $1,000 setup charge apply. Using only these fictional amounts, what is the expected first-month net contribution?

options.text: $5,510, after applying observed adoption to handling benefit and rework, then subtracting the recurring monthly service fee.
options.why: This omits the one-time charge from the requested first month.

options.text: $6,430, after applying handling benefit and rework to every monthly request and subtracting the service fee and setup charge.
options.why: This assumes 100% adoption instead of the observed 75%.

options.text: $5,950, after applying observed adoption to handling benefit and then subtracting the monthly service fee and setup charge.
options.why: This omits the $1,440 expected review/rework cost.

options.text: $4,510, after applying observed adoption to handling benefit and rework, then subtracting the service fee and setup charge.

questions.decision: Apply adoption consistently to both variable benefit and variable rework, and include one-time charges in the stated accounting period.

questions.title: Recovery without repeating side effects
questions.stem: A travel assistant reserves a scarce appointment slot, gathers missing details, and then confirms the booking. Users may disconnect for hours; a confirmation retry sometimes creates a duplicate booking. The reservation expires after a documented interval, and payment is outside this workflow. Which THREE design elements are needed to make the process resumable while respecting the reservation's lifecycle?

options.text: Persist explicit workflow state with the reservation identifier, expiry and completed step results, rather than relying on conversational recall.
options.why: Durable state supports resumption against actual reservation status.

options.text: Regenerate the complete plan from the latest user message and repeat previous operations whenever their results are absent from model context.
options.why: Missing context does not imply an operation failed.

options.text: Use a stable booking operation key and reconcile an uncertain confirmation result with the booking service before issuing another creation request.
options.why: This prevents retrying an already completed side effect.

options.text: Extend every reservation indefinitely whenever an assistant session remains in storage, prioritizing conversational continuity over expiry enforcement.
options.why: Indefinite holds violate the stated reservation lifecycle.

options.text: Check reservation validity on resumption and route expired reservations through a defined reacquisition or user-choice step.
options.why: Expired prerequisites cannot authorize continuation of confirmation.

questions.decision: Resumption requires durable business state, idempotent effects and explicit expiry handling; model memory is insufficient.

questions.title: When abstention is the product behavior
questions.stem: An industrial assistant compares technician notes with machine manuals. It cannot diagnose unseen equipment, and the business explicitly prohibits unsupported maintenance instructions. Technicians still find exact manual excerpts useful when a diagnosis is unavailable. A proposed success metric counts every abstention as failure, encouraging confident guesses. Which architecture and acceptance change BEST preserves useful assistance under the stated boundary?

options.text: Route unsupported diagnoses to a stronger model and allow only its high-confidence instructions, keeping the same diagnosis-coverage success target.
options.why: Unvalidated confidence does not establish support for unseen equipment.

options.text: Keep supported excerpts and abstention, but retain the current metric that penalizes every unavailable diagnosis as a failed interaction.
options.why: The metric still rewards pressure to exceed the supported boundary.

options.text: Return supported manual excerpts and explicit diagnosis limits; evaluate useful evidence delivery separately from unsupported-diagnosis coverage.
options.why: This aligns success with the permitted useful assistance.

options.text: Return supported excerpts and escalate every case to a technician before showing them, measuring success only when a final diagnosis exists.
options.why: It preserves safety but withholds already useful permitted evidence unnecessarily.

questions.decision: Define success around the supported decision boundary, including useful refusal and evidence delivery where diagnosis is unavailable.

questions.title: Delegation with asymmetric authority
questions.stem: An incident coordinator delegates log analysis to specialists for database, network and application layers. A database specialist recommends restarting a production cluster, but only the incident commander may authorize disruptive actions. The coordinator currently forwards recommendations as executable tool calls. Investigations need to remain concurrent. Which change BEST maintains useful delegation while respecting authority and preserving uncertainty?

options.text: Require specialist findings with evidence and uncertainty; let the coordinator propose actions that an execution gateway checks against commander authorization.
options.why: Analysis remains concurrent while action authority stays explicit.

options.text: Require a second specialist to agree with each restart recommendation and treat that agreement as delegated commander authorization.
options.why: Peer agreement does not confer the commander's authority.

options.text: Give every specialist restart privileges during major incidents and require it to document the reasoning after executing its recommendation.
options.why: Post-action explanation cannot replace prior required authorization.

options.text: Remove specialist analysis and place all raw logs into one coordinator prompt so operational authority becomes implicit in the architecture.
options.why: Centralizing analysis does not implement an authorization check.

questions.decision: Delegation transfers bounded analysis responsibility, not automatically the principal's operational permissions.

questions.title: Comparing genuinely different business bets
questions.stem: An airport has funding for one six-week AI pilot. The operations team proposes summarizing shift handovers; security proposes autonomous threat screening; finance proposes drafting routine invoice explanations. The sponsor wants measurable near-term benefit with tolerable deployment risk, and each proposal has a different data-readiness level. Which TWO inputs are most necessary before ranking the proposals?

options.text: A shared requirement that all proposals replace an entire workflow autonomously so their business outcomes use a consistent operating model.
options.why: Uniform autonomy adds unjustified risk and distorts scope.

options.text: A count of how many employees expressed enthusiasm for each idea during the latest internal AI-awareness workshop.
options.why: Enthusiasm is not validated benefit or readiness evidence.

options.text: A benchmark ranking of available models and the maximum context window supported by each proposed technical implementation.
options.why: Model specifications alone cannot rank business feasibility or value.

options.text: Evidence of data availability, decision consequences and integration readiness for each proposal within the six-week delivery constraint.
options.why: These determine feasibility and the risk of the initial scope.

options.text: A baseline workflow measure, reachable target and accountable business owner for each proposal, including how benefit will be observed during the pilot.
options.why: These make unlike proposals comparable on business outcomes.

questions.decision: Compare bounded outcome hypotheses and readiness; selecting a model cannot resolve missing business discovery.

questions.title: Keeping computations outside prose
questions.stem: An energy broker wants explanations of monthly settlements. Meter readings and tariff calculations already exist in a tested accounting service, including unusual rounding rules. A prototype asks Claude to recompute the invoice while explaining it and produces small financial discrepancies. The client needs understandable explanations and exact agreement with the ledger. Which boundary BEST addresses both requirements without duplicating the accounting logic?

options.text: Retrieve signed calculation results and line-item provenance from the accounting service, then generate explanations validated against those authoritative values.
options.why: Exact computation remains in its tested authoritative component.

options.text: Move all tariff logic into a long system prompt and version that prompt alongside the accounting service's existing release notes.
options.why: Duplicating logic in prose creates another inconsistent implementation.

options.text: Provide several examples of settlement rounding and ask Claude to regenerate the complete calculation before writing its explanation.
options.why: Examples do not reproduce every accounting invariant reliably.

options.text: Run two independent models over the readings and publish the explanation when their computed totals agree within a small tolerance.
options.why: Agreement and tolerance do not guarantee ledger equality.

questions.decision: Separate deterministic financial truth from language generation; validate references without reimplementing the trusted computation.

questions.title: A model upgrade with a segment failure
questions.stem: A contract-summary service evaluates two models on the same held-out set. Model Vale improves overall legal-issue recall but misses more termination clauses in short handwritten scans. That segment is a contractual release gate. Model Reed is slower but meets every segment gate within the existing latency budget. Infrastructure and retrieval are identical. What is the BEST production choice while investigating the upgrade?

options.text: Keep Reed for the gated workload, investigate Vale's scan failures, and require segment-level regression acceptance before upgrading.
options.why: The existing model satisfies every binding release requirement.

options.text: Switch fully to Vale because its higher overall recall demonstrates a net improvement across the customer population.
options.why: Aggregate improvement does not override a failing contractual gate.

options.text: Switch to Vale for scanned contracts and Reed for typed contracts because specialization generally improves routed system performance.
options.why: The proposed routing assigns the weaker model to its failing segment.

options.text: Increase Vale's temperature for all contracts and release immediately if a small demonstration fixes one handwritten termination example.
options.why: One stochastic example is inadequate evidence for a critical segment.

questions.decision: Select against workload-specific gates, not model rank or aggregate improvement; routing needs evidence for its assigned slices.

questions.title: Tenant variation without prompt drift
questions.stem: A SaaS writing assistant serves multiple regulated customers. Core safety policy is shared; customers can choose approved tone and terminology, but cannot alter retention, permitted actions or escalation rules. Customer-success staff currently edit copies of the entire system prompt, causing conflicting variants. Which TWO changes BEST preserve controlled customization while making releases testable across tenants?

options.text: Test the composition on policy-conflict and tenant-specific cases, recording both core and tenant configuration versions for each release.
options.why: This checks boundaries and makes variants reproducible.

options.text: Let customer-success staff replace any policy paragraph if the customer signs off on the complete resulting prompt.
options.why: Customer approval cannot override platform restrictions.

options.text: Compose a versioned core policy with schema-validated tenant configuration limited to approved tone and terminology fields.
options.why: It separates permitted variation from protected policy.

options.text: Maintain separate unversioned prompts for each tenant so urgent customization can bypass the shared regression process.
options.why: Unversioned copies perpetuate the drift being addressed.

options.text: Append tenant instructions after retrieved documents and rely on recency to resolve every conflict with the shared safety policy.
options.why: Position is not a safe policy-composition mechanism.

questions.decision: Controlled prompt reuse means an explicit extension contract plus regression coverage for composition conflicts.

questions.title: Examples under a fixed prompt budget
questions.stem: A ticket classifier has a fixed allowance of eight few-shot examples. Three candidate sets were built from reviewed training cases and evaluated on the same untouched workload. Policy requires at least 94% overall accuracy and 90% accuracy distinguishing historical complaints from current incidents. Prompt lengths and latency are equal. Which example set is justified by the supplied evidence before a staged rollout?

options.text: Use set A: its highest overall accuracy provides the strongest evidence when the prompt budget is fixed across candidates.
options.why: A's boundary accuracy is below the required 90%.

options.text: Use set B: it meets both required accuracy thresholds within the same example budget, unlike the alternatives.
options.why: B passes both gates; A fails the boundary and C the aggregate.

options.text: Use set C: its highest boundary accuracy should override the overall requirement because that confusion originally motivated the experiment.
options.why: C misses the independent overall gate.

options.text: Combine all three sets and retain their measured scores, assuming more examples cannot lower either accuracy metric.
options.why: Combining exceeds the budget and invalidates those measurements.

questions.decision: Example selection is a measured constrained decision; a targeted improvement must still satisfy independent release requirements.

questions.title: A correct summary with expired external facts
questions.stem: A maintenance agent resumes after a two-day pause. Its compacted state correctly preserves the user restriction against compressor shutdown, the approved task and every pending approval. However, the plan assumes a spare part remains available and a weather window remains open; both came from time-sensitive tools. No operation has executed. Which resumption action BEST addresses the remaining context risk without rebuilding all historical conversation?

options.text: Discard all preserved task state and re-read every transcript before making any tool call, regardless of which facts are time-sensitive.
options.why: The preserved constraints are sound; targeted revalidation is sufficient.

options.text: Revalidate the time-sensitive prerequisites against current authoritative tools before continuing the preserved plan and its unchanged authority constraints.
options.why: The authority survived; the external facts may have expired.

options.text: Ask the user to repeat the compressor restriction, then continue using the saved spare-part and weather information unchanged.
options.why: Reconfirming authority does not refresh the stale prerequisites.

options.text: Continue immediately because a faithful compacted summary establishes that every fact needed by the approved plan remains valid.
options.why: Faithful historical state does not imply present availability.

questions.decision: Resumption must distinguish durable task authority from expiring external evidence; compaction correctness does not imply data freshness.

questions.title: Cache misses after a tool catalog rollout
questions.stem: A benefits assistant already puts its stable policy before dynamic content and consistently records cache reads under steady traffic. Immediately after a deployment, first calls for each worker record cache writes. Traces show the non-deferred tool catalog changed version while policy text and tenant mapping stayed identical. Subsequent calls reuse the cache. Which TWO conclusions BEST follow from this evidence?

options.text: Increase output-token limits because generated response length determines whether the preceding input prefix can match its previous version.
options.why: Output length does not determine input-prefix equality.

options.text: The changed catalog is a plausible prefix-identity change; compare exact serialized tool and prompt content rather than moving already-correct dynamic fields.
options.why: Tool definitions participate in prefix identity.

options.text: Remove tenant policy addenda immediately because a deployment-associated miss proves tenant isolation prevents all useful caching.
options.why: The evidence identifies a catalog change, not universal tenant incompatibility.

options.text: Move the already trailing request identifier into the system policy to prevent new workers from creating independent cache identities.
options.why: A unique leading field would worsen prefix stability.

options.text: Treat first-call writes after the change as expected warm-up and measure sustained read rates before declaring a continuing cache configuration defect.
options.why: Later reads indicate reuse recovers under the new prefix.

questions.decision: Diagnose actual prefix identity and warm-up behavior; do not repeat generic ordering fixes when ordering is already correct.

questions.title: Reasoning effort versus the actual failure
questions.stem: An analyst asks for three figures from a supplied annual report. The model returns convincing calculations using a similarly named company mentioned in a footnote. The relevant table is present, and arithmetic checks pass when supplied the correct figures. Response latency is already near its limit. Which next experiment BEST targets the observed failure rather than increasing general reasoning cost?

options.text: Add a second arithmetic checker that recomputes the final answer from the first model's extracted figures without checking their source.
options.why: It validates calculations over the wrong inputs.

options.text: Require evidence selection tied to the requested entity and reporting period, then validate calculations over those cited table values.
options.why: The failure concerns source selection, not arithmetic ability.

options.text: Switch to a smaller model and reduce the report to its first page to create additional latency headroom.
options.why: The relevant table may be discarded and selection remains uncontrolled.

options.text: Increase reasoning effort on every request and require a longer explanation before the same unconstrained figure extraction step.
options.why: More reasoning does not target the incorrect entity selection.

questions.decision: Localize the failing stage before paying for broader reasoning; correct arithmetic cannot rescue misidentified evidence.

questions.title: A reusable Skill with a mutable dependency
questions.stem: A team packages an invoice-review procedure as a Skill. The procedure loads a tax table maintained by finance, but the table changes independently of the Skill. A recent regression cannot be reproduced from the Skill version alone. The organization needs reuse across teams and traceable decisions. Which TWO changes BEST address reproducibility while preserving the shared procedure?

options.text: Record the procedure version and the resolved tax-table version or digest in each review's auditable execution metadata.
options.why: Both code-like procedure and data dependency determine behavior.

options.text: Pin the Skill procedure version and keep resolving the latest tax table, recording only the procedure in the audit trail.
options.why: The changing resolved dependency remains unrecorded and unreproducible.

options.text: Copy the newest tax table into every analyst's personal Skill directory and let each analyst update it when convenient.
options.why: Uncoordinated copies create additional untracked variants.

options.text: Treat the Skill version as sufficient provenance because supporting files are implementation details rather than decision inputs.
options.why: The changing file directly affects the decision.

options.text: Define compatibility and regression checks when the shared tax-table dependency changes, with a controlled promotion process for affected teams.
options.why: This validates changes without cloning the procedure per team.

questions.decision: Reusable procedures still need dependency provenance and controlled data promotion; a versioned wrapper alone is insufficient.

questions.title: A cache-rate break-even calculation
questions.stem: A service sends a 10,000-token prefix on each request. Use fictional prices: ordinary input costs $3 per million tokens, a cache write costs $3.75 per million, and a cache read costs $0.30 per million. Each request is either one write or one read for the entire prefix; ignore other tokens and storage fees. At what read-hit rate does expected prefix cost equal ordinary uncached cost?

options.text: Approximately 10.00% read hits; greater hit rates make the expected prefix-token charge lower than ordinary uncached input.
options.why: This compares read and ordinary prices without including write overhead.

options.text: Approximately 21.74% read hits; greater hit rates make the expected prefix-token charge lower than ordinary uncached input.
Approximately 80.00% read hits; greater hit rates make the expected prefix-token charge lower than ordinary uncached input.
options.why: This does not solve the stated weighted-cost equation.

options.text: Approximately 25.00% read hits; greater hit rates make the expected prefix-token charge lower than ordinary uncached input.
options.why: The write premium percentage is not the weighted break-even rate.

questions.decision: Account for both cache writes and reads; the break-even rate is write premium divided by the write-read price difference.

questions.title: Discovery without expanding privilege
questions.stem: A claims analyst needs six tools daily and occasionally one of seventy specialist read-only tools. A migration to tool search reduced prompt size, but the catalog also exposes account-maintenance tools that analysts are forbidden to use. The team argues discovery is safe because those tools are not loaded until requested. Which configuration BEST combines context efficiency with the role's capability boundary?

options.text: Defer the maintenance tools and mark their descriptions as administrative, relying on low discovery frequency as the access control.
options.why: Rare discovery is not an authorization control.

options.text: Load all ninety tool definitions directly and ask the model to select the six allowed tools based on its current task.
options.why: This loses context efficiency and leaves forbidden tools available.

options.text: Keep every tool discoverable and add descriptions instructing the model to avoid maintenance operations unless a user insists.
options.why: Descriptions do not remove prohibited capabilities.

options.text: Expose only authorized tools in the role's discoverable catalog, keeping frequent tools direct and eligible specialist tools deferred.
options.why: Discovery controls context loading; the catalog still needs role scoping.

questions.decision: Reduce authorized context volume and unauthorized capability separately; deferred availability does not imply least privilege.

questions.title: Resource-bound access tokens
questions.stem: A remote MCP client obtains a token intended for the document server. A reporting server accepts it because both servers trust the same issuer and the token is unexpired. Users can consequently retrieve reports beyond the document service's intended boundary. The client also omits resource identification during token acquisition. Which TWO changes most directly repair the cross-resource authentication gap?

options.text: Move the token into a request query parameter so the reporting server can log the exact credential used by the client.
options.why: Query placement adds exposure without fixing audience validation.

options.text: Shorten document-token lifetimes while continuing to accept the same token at every server managed by the trusted issuer.
options.why: Shorter validity leaves the resource-confusion flaw intact.

options.text: Have the client identify the intended MCP resource in authorization and token requests using the server's canonical resource URI.
options.why: This requests a token bound to the intended resource.

options.text: Require model-generated explanations of why a report is relevant before the reporting server accepts document-server credentials.
options.why: Relevance explanations do not establish token audience.

options.text: Have each MCP resource server validate the token's intended audience in addition to issuer, validity and applicable permissions.
options.why: A trusted issuer alone does not bind a token to this server.

questions.decision: Tokens must be requested for and validated by their intended resource; shared identity infrastructure does not collapse resource boundaries.

questions.title: A genuine scope gap rather than expiry
questions.stem: A document-editing MCP call fails after a successful read operation. The token remains valid and targets the correct server. The response indicates insufficient scope and advertises the write permission required by that operation. The user has requested an edit, but organizational policy requires consent for newly requested write privileges. Which client behavior BEST handles the failure without unnecessarily repeating the task or enlarging access? The workflow still needs its existing read permission after editing.

options.text: Obtain consent for the server's full advertised administrative scope set, then retry with one token to avoid future permission interruptions.
options.why: The scope expansion exceeds the operation's demonstrated need.

options.text: Obtain consent for the additional required write scope, retain still-needed read grants, and retry the operation after authorization succeeds.
options.why: This satisfies controlled step-up without dropping existing needed access.

options.text: Obtain consent for write scope only and replace the previous grant set, then retry the edit without checking later read requirements.
options.why: It can fix the edit while breaking the still-required read operation.

options.text: Repeat protected-resource discovery and retry with the same read-only grant, because valid metadata is sufficient to authorize advertised operations.
options.why: Discovery describes permissions; it does not confer the missing grant.

questions.decision: Diagnose the actual authorization failure; a valid token can still lack the operation's required consented scope.

questions.title: Correlation without sensitive payload capture
questions.stem: A multi-tenant assistant calls a retriever, a model and two external services. End-to-end p95 rose after a rollout, while each vendor dashboard's median remains stable. Support needs tenant-specific diagnosis, but policy forbids storing raw customer prompts in routine telemetry. Which THREE additions BEST make the regression diagnosable under those constraints?

options.text: Average vendor medians into one health score and page the vendor with the highest average after each release.
options.why: Averages of medians cannot locate an end-to-end tail regression.

options.text: Provide restricted diagnostic sampling of redacted events and assign alert thresholds and incident ownership for affected service objectives.
options.why: Bounded evidence and response ownership make telemetry operationally useful.

options.text: Propagate a pseudonymous request correlation identifier through orchestrator and dependency spans, with prompt and model version labels.
options.why: Correlation links stages without requiring raw prompt content.

options.text: Record complete prompts, retrieved documents and access tokens on every request so support can reproduce failures without further approval.
options.why: The proposed capture violates the telemetry restriction and exposes credentials.

options.text: Measure end-to-end and stage tail distributions, including queue time, retries and errors, segmented by authorized operational dimensions.
options.why: Tail and queue measures reveal what medians conceal.

questions.decision: Observe the user journey and correlated stages while minimizing content; diagnostic convenience cannot override telemetry restrictions.

questions.title: Parallelism with a dependent step
questions.stem: An approval assistant performs identity lookup and credit-policy retrieval, then evaluates eligibility using both results. The trace shows identity takes 0.8 seconds, policy retrieval 1.2 seconds and evaluation 0.9 seconds. Calls are currently sequential. Assume these fixed durations, no contention and negligible orchestration overhead. Which redesign and predicted critical-path duration are supported before validating real production tails?

options.text: Run identity lookup and eligibility evaluation concurrently after policy retrieval; the modeled critical path becomes 2.1 seconds.
options.why: Eligibility still needs identity's result before it can run.

options.text: Run identity lookup and policy retrieval concurrently, then evaluate eligibility; the modeled critical path becomes 2.1 seconds.
Run all three steps concurrently and combine their results afterward; the modeled critical path becomes 1.2 seconds.
options.why: Evaluation depends on both reads and cannot start independently.

options.text: Run the two reads concurrently but retain the sum of all durations; the modeled critical path remains 2.9 seconds.
options.why: It incorrectly adds durations of independent concurrent reads.

questions.decision: Respect the dependency graph when predicting latency; modeled critical paths are hypotheses, not production percentile guarantees.

questions.title: Correct chunks, wrong revision comparison
questions.stem: A technical-manual RAG pipeline already preserves section headings, product metadata and warnings. Users ask what changed between firmware revisions 8 and 9. The retriever applies a newest-only filter, so the generator receives correct revision-9 chunks but invents the old behavior. The latency budget permits two bounded retrievals. Which change BEST targets the failure without undoing the existing chunk design?

options.text: Remove all version filters and select the most similar passages, asking the generator to infer which revision each statement belongs to.
options.why: Unlabeled mixed evidence can create another revision-confusion failure.

options.text: Rechunk every manual into smaller passages, retaining the same newest-only filter so retrieval becomes more precise within revision 9.
options.why: Chunk precision is not the missing revision source.

options.text: Increase revision-9 top-k while retaining the newest-only filter, giving the generator more context about the current product behavior.
options.why: More current evidence cannot establish the old behavior.

options.text: Retrieve aligned evidence from both requested revisions, label versions explicitly and require comparisons to cite each side or report missing evidence.
options.why: The comparative task requires both historical and current evidence.

questions.decision: Match the retrieval contract to a cross-version question; correct current chunks do not support a historical comparison.

questions.title: An exact match lost after retrieval
questions.stem: A parts assistant already uses hybrid retrieval. Candidate recall tests show the correct exact part identifier appears in the initial twenty results, but a semantic reranker drops it below the final four when descriptive neighbors sound more relevant. The final evidence budget cannot exceed four chunks. Which TWO changes BEST target the failing stage without paying for a larger generator context?

options.text: Inspect reranker features and preserve verified exact-identifier candidates through an appropriate ranking rule for identifier-bearing queries.
options.why: The exact evidence is lost at ranking, not initial retrieval.

options.text: Evaluate final evidence recall separately from candidate recall on identifier and descriptive query slices under the four-chunk budget.
options.why: This measures the stage-specific repair and its trade-off.

options.text: Add a larger generator while keeping the same four incorrect final chunks, expecting stronger reasoning to recover the missing exact record.
options.why: The generator still lacks the required record.

options.text: Replace hybrid retrieval with dense-only retrieval because the exact identifier's low final rank proves lexical candidate generation is ineffective.
options.why: Candidate generation is working; final ranking drops the match.

options.text: Increase the initial candidate pool to one hundred and keep the same reranker, assuming candidate recall is the measured bottleneck.
options.why: The correct candidate already reaches the reranker.

questions.decision: Measure and repair the stage that loses correct evidence; high candidate recall can coexist with poor final evidence recall.

questions.title: A protocol decision with an existing batch interface
questions.stem: A nightly reconciliation job invokes one internal service with a stable typed endpoint and service-to-service authentication. It has no interactive tool selection, and the operations team already monitors the API. A proposal introduces an MCP server and an agent to choose reconciliation operations dynamically, adding another deployment to support. Which integration decision BEST follows the current requirements and operational constraints?

options.text: Wrap the same typed API in MCP with identical authentication, adding catalog discovery and a second deployment for this one fixed caller.
options.why: The added discovery layer offers no required benefit for this job.

options.text: Use an agent-to-agent task service with the same authentication, adding clarification and delegated planning states to the nightly reconciliation contract.
options.why: The fixed operation does not require delegated planning or clarification.

options.text: Expose both direct API and MCP routes immediately with identical permissions, requiring operations to support both until future users choose a preference.
options.why: Duplicated operating paths are unjustified by the current single-caller requirement.

options.text: Retain the typed API in the existing batch workflow, using scoped service authentication and current monitoring ownership.
options.why: The existing mechanism already meets the stated noninteractive boundary.

questions.decision: Choose the integration mechanism for the boundary's actual needs; standardization does not automatically justify a new runtime layer.

questions.title: Progressive discovery and exact definitions
questions.stem: A platform offers hundreds of optional tools. The team enables deferred tool loading but removes the deferred tools' definitions from the request entirely, expecting search to reconstruct schemas from tool names. Discovery returns references that cannot be expanded correctly. The current API's documented tool-search contract requires server-side definitions for the catalog. Which TWO changes BEST repair the integration while keeping context small?

options.text: Grant the discovery service permission to invoke unregistered tool names whenever a textual description appears sufficiently relevant.
options.why: Unregistered execution breaks the explicit configured capability boundary.

options.text: Remove all schemas permanently and ask the model to invent argument structures from the names of search results.
options.why: Invented schemas cannot satisfy the integration contract.

options.text: Keep the discovery entry point and frequent tools directly available, then verify returned references resolve to configured definitions.
options.why: This preserves discoverability and reference integrity.

options.text: Load every optional definition directly into model context so returned references become unnecessary for all future tasks.
options.why: It abandons the stated context-efficiency requirement.

options.text: Include full eligible deferred tool definitions in the request catalog while marking them for deferred context loading as documented.
options.why: Deferred context loading does not remove server-side catalog requirements.

questions.decision: Deferred loading changes when definitions enter model context; it does not eliminate the catalog contract.

questions.title: Authorization after a document move
questions.stem: A merger moves confidential policy documents from one department to another. The source repository updates permissions immediately, but the RAG index refreshes overnight. Search candidates still contain old access metadata, and cached answers remain valid for one day. The business requires immediate denial after access removal. Which design BEST closes both stale-index and answer-cache exposure paths?

options.text: Recheck current authorization before returning evidence or cached answers, and invalidate or scope caches by authorization and document-version state.
options.why: Current enforcement prevents stale derived artifacts from granting access.

options.text: Add a confidentiality warning to retrieved excerpts whenever their cached metadata indicates that a document recently changed departments.
options.why: Warnings do not deny access to removed principals.

options.text: Shorten index refresh to hourly and assume all cached answers remain authorized until their ordinary one-day expiration.
options.why: An hour still violates immediate denial and cached answers remain exposed.

options.text: Encrypt the index at rest and keep existing authorization checks only during document ingestion to reduce per-query latency.
options.why: At-rest encryption does not enforce current reader authorization.

questions.decision: An asynchronously refreshed search artifact cannot be the sole authority for an immediate revocation requirement.

questions.title: A tail regression hidden by streaming
questions.stem: A customer endpoint advertises a five-second completed-answer SLA. Enabling streaming reduces first-token latency from 1.1 to 0.3 seconds but leaves p95 completion at 6.2 seconds. Users also wait for a final signed citation bundle before acting. The team proposes declaring the SLA met based on the new first-token metric. Which response BEST aligns the configuration decision with the actual service obligation?

options.text: Negotiate a longer completion target for a future contract revision, counting current 6.2-second completions as compliant before the revision is accepted.
options.why: A proposed future change does not alter the current obligation.

options.text: Introduce an interim acknowledgment target and describe it clearly, but report the existing completed-answer SLA as met by that acknowledgment.
options.why: A useful new interim target does not satisfy the unchanged completion SLA.

options.text: Keep the five-second validated-completion obligation and treat streaming as a separate usability gain while optimizing the measured completion bottleneck.
options.why: It reports the current breach honestly and preserves the agreed endpoint.

options.text: Keep final signed citations but report generation-end latency before citation assembly as the completed-answer metric under the original contract.
options.why: The user cannot act until the required citation bundle completes.

questions.decision: User-perceived responsiveness and actionable completion are distinct metrics; keep the promised endpoint explicit.

questions.title: An expired retry key after a completed effect
questions.stem: A shipment API retains idempotency keys for one day. A release call timed out, but later reconciliation proved the warehouse completed the release. Three days later a support worker reopens the assistant conversation and asks it to finish the original release. The saved task still shows pending because reconciliation was not persisted. Which TWO changes BEST prevent a duplicate while repairing the workflow state?

options.text: Persist terminal business status and reconciliation evidence independently of the API's limited idempotency-retention window.
options.why: Durable business state must outlive transport deduplication.

options.text: Create a fresh idempotency key for the old request, treating the reopened conversation as proof of a new shipment-release intent.
options.why: Reopening the old task does not authorize another release.

options.text: Consult the reconciled business-operation record and mark the original release complete, rather than replaying its now-expired transport idempotency key.
options.why: The business effect is already known to have occurred.

options.text: Cancel the completed shipment automatically to restore the saved pending state before rerunning the original release flow.
options.why: The recorded state should be repaired to match reality.

options.text: Replay the original idempotency key because identical keys always prevent duplicate effects regardless of the provider's documented retention interval.
options.why: The deduplication window has expired.

questions.decision: A transport retry guarantee has a finite scope; durable terminal business truth prevents replay after that guarantee expires.

questions.title: Measuring an assisted outcome
questions.stem: A pathology-report assistant drafts summaries for specialists. The product team reports 97% fluent summaries and lower API cost. Clinicians care about missed actionable findings, review time and safe handling of ambiguous terminology. Deployment policy requires independent safety acceptance even if productivity improves. Which measurement plan BEST supports a defensible release decision across those competing objectives?

options.text: Measure critical omissions, review time and cost only among accepted drafts, excluding rejected or escalated cases from every denominator.
options.why: The selected denominator conceals unsuccessful workload and its review burden.

options.text: Measure actionable-finding recall, harmful omissions, clinician review time and per-completed-case cost, applying an independent critical-error gate.
options.why: It covers consequence, clinical usefulness and realized productivity economics.

options.text: Measure actionable-finding recall, fluency, model-call cost and generation latency, applying the independent critical-error gate before release.
options.why: It omits actual review effort and substitutes component economics for case economics.

options.text: Measure clinician satisfaction, review time, completed-case cost and overall summary accuracy, pooling critical and routine findings into one accuracy target.
options.why: Pooling loses the independent critical-error requirement.

questions.decision: Choose metrics tied to the decision and consequence; independent safety gates cannot be traded away through a weighted average.

questions.title: Mixed graders with different jobs
questions.stem: A research agent must find three supported facts, avoid restricted sources and produce a usable briefing. Exact wording varies. The current grader accepts any briefing containing three expected keywords, even if citations are fabricated. Domain experts can review a small sample, but cannot read every run. Which TWO changes BEST improve validity while keeping the framework scalable?

options.text: Grade only the agent's planning narrative because a well-structured plan demonstrates that the final cited facts are reliable.
options.why: The plan does not establish the final claims or actual source use.

options.text: Require the briefing to quote the expected answer verbatim and reject any alternate wording as a factual error.
options.why: Exact wording is not the supported-fact requirement.

options.text: Add deterministic checks for source access policy and citation resolvability, plus a grounded-support rubric for the substantive claims.
options.why: Different graders address verifiable constraints and semantic support.

options.text: Replace the keyword grader with another model that assigns an overall score without explicit criteria or expert comparison.
options.why: An uncalibrated holistic score is difficult to trust.

options.text: Calibrate the semantic grader against expert-labeled examples and periodically inspect disagreement slices and changed configurations.
options.why: Human calibration detects systematic judge errors and drift.

questions.decision: Use each grading method where it is valid, and validate semantic judgment against accountable domain expertise.

questions.title: An A/B result with shifting traffic
questions.stem: A retrieval change launches to the morning support queue while the old system serves evenings. The morning queue handles mostly routine domestic cases; evening traffic includes complex international cases. The new system has a higher success rate, but no customer or case-type adjustment was made. Both variants use the same model. Which next experiment BEST isolates the retrieval change's effect?

options.text: Randomize comparable traffic to variants at a stable unit, balance important case slices, and keep other configuration and success definitions fixed.
options.why: This reduces assignment confounding while isolating retrieval.

options.text: Run the new system for another morning week and accept the result if its aggregate success rate stays above evenings.
options.why: Repeating the confounded assignment does not remove bias.

options.text: Compare only customer satisfaction from completed cases, excluding unresolved cases so differences in queue complexity cannot affect the result.
options.why: Excluding failures introduces selection bias.

options.text: Upgrade the new variant's model while extending its operating hours, then compare its total successful case count with the old variant.
options.why: Multiple changes and exposure differences obscure attribution.

questions.decision: Comparable randomized exposure and stable definitions are needed before interpreting an observed aggregate difference causally.

questions.title: A prompt change is not an index fix
questions.stem: After an index migration, an employee assistant returns last year's travel limits. Traces show the generator faithfully quotes retrieved chunks tagged with the new ingestion timestamp, but source revision identifiers still refer to archived policy. The model and prompt are unchanged. Which initial diagnostic action BEST distinguishes the suspected pipeline defect before attempting a generation-side repair?

options.text: Replace the model immediately because correctly quoting outdated chunks demonstrates insufficient reasoning over policy recency.
options.why: Faithful use of stale evidence indicates an upstream problem.

options.text: Increase generation temperature so the assistant is less likely to repeat the exact outdated limits quoted in its context.
options.why: Randomness does not restore current authoritative evidence.

options.text: Compare active source revisions with indexed payloads and ingestion lineage, then test whether stale content was re-labeled rather than replaced.
options.why: The evidence points to stale indexed content with fresh ingestion metadata.

options.text: Increase the system prompt's emphasis on current information and keep the same retrieved evidence and ingestion process unchanged.
options.why: Instructions cannot supply a missing current policy.

questions.decision: Differentiate ingestion time from source validity; inspect the failing lineage before changing the component behaving as configured.

questions.title: Routing cost with full-system quality
questions.stem: A team proposes routing simple cases to a cheaper model and complex cases to a stronger model. Isolated model benchmarks look favorable, but routing errors can send complex cases down the cheap path, causing escalations and extra calls. Finance wants lower cost per successfully completed case without reducing critical-case quality. Which TWO evaluation additions are most necessary?

options.text: Evaluate the complete router-plus-model system on representative cases, including misroutes and critical-slice outcomes against the existing quality gates.
options.why: Component benchmarks miss routing-induced failures.

options.text: Estimate savings from the cheap model's input-token price and assume the router's declared confidence is calibrated across every case type.
options.why: Price and unvalidated confidence omit system failures.

options.text: Route all cases cheaply during the test and add stronger-model calls only after customer complaints indicate a missed critical issue.
options.why: It exposes users before validating the critical gate.

options.text: Exclude escalated cases from both cost and quality metrics because their resolution occurs outside the model-routing service.
options.why: This hides the cost and quality impact being evaluated.

options.text: Include retries, escalations, tool charges and human recovery in cost per completed acceptable outcome, rather than comparing nominal model prices.
options.why: This measures realized system economics.

questions.decision: Evaluate routing as part of the product and price successful outcomes, including recovery, rather than isolated successful calls.

questions.title: Sampling that misses the outage
questions.stem: An assistant's routine logs sample one percent of requests uniformly. A new tool version fails only for a small tenant with a rare permission configuration; the global error rate barely moves and sampled traces miss the failure. Policy permits metadata but limits content retention. Which monitoring change BEST makes this failure class visible without storing every request payload?

options.text: Suppress tenant-level metrics until each tenant has the same traffic volume so aggregate alerts remain statistically comparable.
options.why: That would conceal the affected small tenant.

options.text: Monitor only the model provider's aggregate status because permission configuration is an application concern outside AI observability.
options.why: Application integration failures affect the delivered service.

options.text: Retain error and critical-slice metadata preferentially, track per-tenant/version denominators and alert on slice failure rates with controlled diagnostic sampling.
options.why: This targets rare failures while preserving meaningful exposure counts.

options.text: Increase uniform content sampling to two percent and retain all sampled prompts indefinitely to improve the chance of catching unusual cases.
options.why: It still lacks targeted visibility and exceeds retention needs.

questions.decision: Sampling should reflect consequence and rarity; keep denominators and targeted metadata so uncommon failures remain detectable.

questions.title: Weighting performance without waiving a risk gate
questions.stem: A document assistant is tested on two slices. Ordinary documents are 98% of production and achieve 95% correctness; forged documents are 2% and achieve 60%. The evaluation set contains equal numbers of each. The business requires at least 94% workload-weighted correctness and at least 70% correctness on forged-document handling. Using these fictional figures, which release interpretation is supported?

options.text: Workload-weighted correctness is 94.3%, so the release passes because the small forged-document population is already reflected in that weighted figure.
options.why: Weighting does not waive the separate slice gate.

options.text: Workload-weighted correctness is 95%, so the release passes because ordinary traffic dominates and forged cases can be treated as outliers.
options.why: Rare cases still contribute and have their own requirement.

options.text: Workload-weighted correctness is 94.3%, but the release still fails the independent forged-document gate despite passing the overall threshold.
Workload-weighted correctness is 77.5%, so the release fails both gates because the evaluation contains equal numbers of each slice.
options.why: 77.5% is the deliberately balanced test-set average.

questions.decision: Weight representative performance using prevalence, then apply the independently specified high-risk acceptance criterion.

questions.title: Avoiding repeated-peeking release decisions
questions.stem: A prompt A/B test has a prespecified decision protocol requiring the full planned duration unless the safety stop rule triggers. Product staff check conversion every hour and want to stop at the first favorable result, despite unchanged exposure targets and no safety breach. The cases vary substantially by weekday. Which TWO actions BEST preserve an interpretable experiment while retaining the ability to respond to actual harm?

options.text: Follow the stipulated full-duration decision protocol unless its safety stop condition triggers, rather than choosing a favorable fluctuation.
options.why: The agreed protocol does not authorize stopping on this metric fluctuation.

options.text: Pool only hours where the treatment outperformed control to remove low-volume intervals that make the result appear inconsistent.
options.why: Selective pooling biases the estimate.

options.text: Suspend safety monitoring until the exposure target is reached so every experimental decision follows one fixed stopping rule.
options.why: Safety obligations remain active during experimentation.

options.text: Keep the independent safety stop rule active and report uncertainty and weekday coverage when judging the completed business-outcome comparison.
options.why: Safety intervention need not erase statistical discipline.

options.text: Stop immediately when any hourly conversion chart turns positive and restart the test if the next deployment week is disappointing.
options.why: This selects noise and prevents a stable interpretation.

questions.decision: Follow the explicitly agreed evidence protocol; a business-metric fluctuation is not the stipulated safety stopping condition.

questions.title: Correct answer, unacceptable behavior
questions.stem: A warehouse agent gets the right inventory balance in tests, but inspection shows it queries an unrestricted administrative export and filters the result locally. The intended design permits only item-specific authorized queries. Existing evaluation scores the final numerical answer alone. Which change BEST diagnoses and prevents this false success signal without prescribing every internal reasoning step?

options.text: Continue grading final numbers only because correct filtering means the unauthorized records never appear in the user-facing answer.
options.why: Unauthorized access remains a violation even without display.

options.text: Require every test to match one reference wording and one exact token sequence so hidden administrative exports become impossible.
options.why: Exact text matching neither observes access nor permits valid variation.

options.text: Add checks on actual tool access and data movement alongside final-state correctness, testing permitted alternative trajectories rather than one exact transcript.
options.why: The forbidden access is a behavior constraint independent of answer correctness.

options.text: Require the agent to print a compliance statement before the answer and accept that statement as proof of the permitted query path.
options.why: A self-description does not establish actual tool behavior.

questions.decision: Evaluate external actions and state against explicit constraints; correct final answers do not establish compliant execution.

questions.title: Release gates with a regression owner
questions.stem: An assistant's quality dashboard aggregates all traffic into a rolling monthly score. A release introduces a defect affecting one language, but the monthly average still passes. The customer agreement requires that language to meet its own target, and engineers cannot identify which release changed behavior. Which TWO changes BEST turn monitoring into a usable release-and-response control?

options.text: Track the contractual language slice with its own denominator and gate, retaining model, prompt and retrieval version identifiers.
options.why: This exposes the independent failure and its configuration lineage.

options.text: Assign an owner and rollback or containment procedure for slice breaches, then add resolved cases to the regression suite.
options.why: This connects detection to response and future prevention.

options.text: Add more positive examples from the dominant language to stabilize the overall dashboard before investigating minority-language results.
options.why: That further masks the failing contractual slice.

options.text: Raise the global quality target enough that any future language-specific issue is guaranteed to lower the aggregate below threshold.
options.why: A rare slice can remain hidden in any feasible aggregate.

options.text: Delay new releases until a full month of feedback is available, leaving the affected language on the current failing deployment.
options.why: This does not contain the known breach.

questions.decision: Independent promises need independent visibility and ownership; versioned feedback must lead to containment and regression prevention.

questions.title: Retrieved instructions and an approved workflow
questions.stem: A procurement assistant summarizes vendor proposals and can prepare purchase requests for approval. One proposal contains text asking the assistant to export competing bids to a vendor address, presenting that request as an internal audit requirement. The legitimate user asked only for a comparison. Access to competing bids is valid for comparison, and outputs may later trigger tools. Which control design BEST preserves the useful task while containing this injection path?

options.text: Restrict exports to approved vendor domains and allow proposal-embedded requests whenever the destination passes that domain check.
options.why: An approved destination still lacks authorization for competing bids.

options.text: Remove vendor names from proposals before generation and keep the export tool's broad destination permissions unchanged.
options.why: Anonymization does not prevent instruction-driven exfiltration.

options.text: Let the model classify audit requests and export when two independent model passes agree the language appears organizationally legitimate.
options.why: Model agreement cannot establish external export authority.

options.text: Treat proposal text as evidence, enforce allowed destinations and purpose-bound tool authorization outside the model, and require approval for consequential exports.
options.why: Retrieved instructions cannot extend the user's authorized purpose.

questions.decision: Separate the right to read for comparison from the right to export; evidence content cannot grant a new purpose.

questions.title: A review queue under peak load
questions.stem: A benefits assistant flags disputed cases for mandatory specialist approval before sending decisions. At peak load, the queue exceeds available specialists and users wait past the promised response deadline. Automatic approval is prohibited; the business can offer a non-decision acknowledgment while review proceeds. Which THREE controls BEST manage the operational risk without quietly changing decision authority?

options.text: Use bounded intake or acknowledgment-only fallback when review capacity is exceeded, clearly communicating the pending decision and next response commitment.
options.why: This avoids unapproved decisions during overload.

options.text: Keep accepting every case under the original deadline and average response time across routine cases to demonstrate service compliance.
options.why: Averages conceal the breached obligation for disputed cases.

options.text: Prioritize according to approved consequence and deadline rules while retaining mandatory review and an auditable record of deferred cases.
options.why: Explicit prioritization manages overload without changing authority.

options.text: Forecast review arrival and service rates by case class, reserve specialist capacity and define backlog thresholds with a named escalation owner.
options.why: Capacity evidence is needed to keep mandatory review operable.

options.text: Use model confidence to bypass review for disputed cases during peaks, retaining retrospective specialist audits for accountability.
options.why: Confidence cannot waive a mandatory pre-decision review.

questions.decision: A human control needs capacity, an overload policy and consequence-aware ownership; a queue is not itself a functioning safeguard.

questions.title: A BAA is part of the boundary
questions.stem: A healthcare analytics team has a business associate agreement for a contracted cloud service. It proposes forwarding patient narratives to a separate external debugging service to investigate malformed model output. That service is outside the reviewed agreement and security assessment. The team can reproduce some failures with synthetic cases. Which action BEST handles the immediate investigation while the production data-flow decision is reviewed?

options.text: Obtain the model's assurance that the narratives contain no meaningful identifiers and treat its answer as the required privacy review.
options.why: A model assertion is not an approved de-identification determination.

options.text: Transmit encrypted narratives and provide the debugging service the decryption key under the existing cloud service's support ticket.
options.why: Encryption with recipient access does not remove recipient obligations.

options.text: Transmit the narratives because the original cloud agreement establishes compliance for all downstream services used by the analytics team.
options.why: One agreement does not automatically cover a separate recipient.

options.text: Use synthetic or appropriately de-identified reproductions now, and require assessment of the external service and applicable agreements before transmitting identifiable health data.
options.why: The new recipient is not covered by the existing reviewed boundary.

questions.decision: Review the actual new recipient and data flow; vendor status cannot automatically extend an approved processing boundary.

questions.title: Restoring backups without restoring erased data
questions.stem: A privacy-approved erasure process removes scoped personal records from active stores and maintains deletion tombstones. Encrypted backups have a separately approved retention period and are not available for ordinary queries. During disaster recovery, restoring last month's backup would reintroduce records erased since then. The privacy officer has approved a restoration protocol requiring those erasures to remain effective. Which implementation BEST satisfies that specific obligation?

options.text: Replay applicable deletion tombstones and validate the restored data before reopening ordinary access, retaining the approved backup-retention and audit controls.
options.why: Recovery must preserve erasures made after the backup snapshot.

options.text: Reopen access immediately after restore and wait for affected people to submit new erasure requests before deleting their restored records.
options.why: The approved obligation does not require people to request again.

options.text: Delete every backup immediately even when its approved retention still applies, using the absence of backups as the restoration protocol.
options.why: The stated protocol allows controlled retained backups and recovery.

options.text: Treat restored records as newly collected data and reset their retention clocks because the recovery event generated a new active copy.
options.why: Recovery does not create a new authorized collection purpose.

questions.decision: Backup retention and restored active-data obligations are distinct; replay approved deletion history before restored records become available.

questions.title: Finding evidence gaps in a responsibility matrix
questions.stem: A federal assistant's reviewed control matrix marks physical datacenter security as inherited, application audit forwarding as customer-operated and connector credential rotation as customer-operated. Provider evidence for the inherited control is current. The application team has no test results for forwarding or rotation, but reports that all components use the assured cloud service. Which TWO evidence requests BEST address the actual unresolved controls?

options.text: Request evidence that connector credentials rotate and old credentials are rejected through the defined operational procedure.
options.why: This tests the customer-operated credential lifecycle control.

options.text: Request a new physical datacenter inspection by the application team before considering either of the missing application-control tests.
options.why: Current applicable inherited evidence already covers that control.

options.text: Request a demonstrated application audit event reaching the approved collector with required attribution, access control and incident-owner routing.
options.why: This tests the customer-operated audit control.

options.text: Request another copy of the provider's generic assurance badge and mark all customer-operated controls satisfied when it arrives.
options.why: A badge does not demonstrate the assigned application controls.

options.text: Request only proof that the selected model is the provider's default, treating that configuration as evidence of forwarding and rotation.
options.why: Default model selection does not test either missing control.

questions.decision: Use the established responsibility matrix to seek missing evidence; inherited assurance cannot stand in for untested customer controls.

questions.title: Fairness at the decision boundary
questions.stem: A hiring assistant ranks applicants for human review. Overall qualification recall improves, but candidates from a particular educational pathway are less often surfaced despite equivalent independently assessed qualifications. The pathway is not intended to affect eligibility, and downstream reviewers rarely inspect hidden applicants. Which response BEST addresses the observed fairness risk before broad rollout while retaining meaningful performance evaluation?

options.text: Delete the explicit pathway field and assume fairness is resolved without checking text-derived proxies or subgroup outcomes.
options.why: Equivalent proxies can preserve the disparity.

options.text: Force identical final hiring totals across pathways without examining qualifications, ranking-stage errors or the organization's approved fairness objective.
options.why: Equal totals alone do not establish the relevant decision quality.

options.text: Keep the ranking because final reviewers are human and overall qualification recall increased across the total applicant pool.
options.why: Hidden candidates may never receive meaningful human review.

options.text: Investigate subgroup selection and qualification errors, review proxy features with domain experts, and validate mitigation against both fairness and role-quality criteria.
options.why: It targets the consequential exclusion mechanism and validates trade-offs.

questions.decision: Inspect where opportunity is lost; human review and field removal are not evidence that the ranking is fair.

questions.title: Material and immaterial proposal revisions
questions.stem: A dispatcher approves rerouting shipment X with route R, a four-hour transit ceiling and specified temperature controls. The approval policy says only changes to those material fields require reapproval. Revision A corrects spelling in the customer note; revision B changes the route to five hours while preserving the shipment identity. Which execution rule BEST follows the explicitly defined approval contract?

options.text: Require new approval for both revisions because any changed text proves the approved proposal no longer exists in its original form.
options.why: The policy expressly excludes immaterial changes.

options.text: Keep approval valid for both revisions because the shipment identity remains unchanged and temperature controls are preserved.
options.why: B breaches the approved route and transit condition.

options.text: Approve revision B automatically if the agent explains the delay, but block revision A until the dispatcher verifies the corrected spelling.
options.why: This reverses the specified materiality boundary.

options.text: Keep approval valid for revision A, but block revision B pending new approval of its changed material route and transit terms.
options.why: Only B changes approved risk parameters.

questions.decision: Apply the actual approval contract: avoid unnecessary review of harmless edits while enforcing renewed authority for material changes.

questions.title: Incident containment and safe continuity
questions.stem: A customer assistant begins exposing snippets from another tenant after a cache-key change. The incident is confirmed; the underlying documents remain correctly permissioned. Service owners can disable the shared answer cache and serve authenticated retrieval directly, at higher latency. Which TWO immediate actions BEST limit harm while preserving an investigable recovery path?

options.text: Increase the prompt's confidentiality warning while leaving the shared cache enabled to avoid disrupting normal response times.
options.why: A prompt cannot prevent an incorrect cached answer being served.

options.text: Delete all diagnostic evidence before informing owners so no residual copies of exposed content remain anywhere in the incident system.
options.why: Uncontrolled deletion destroys evidence required for assessment.

options.text: Disable or isolate the affected answer-cache path and use the verified authenticated fallback within a communicated degraded service mode.
options.why: This contains the identified exposure while retaining a safer path.

options.text: Clear the cache once and restore the same keying logic immediately because no incorrect document permissions were found in the source store.
options.why: The flawed keying can recreate cross-tenant exposure.

options.text: Preserve access-controlled incident evidence, assess affected users and data, and coordinate response and notification decisions with responsible security/privacy owners.
