options.why: This supports scoped impact assessment and accountable response.

questions.decision: Contain the demonstrated path first, preserve appropriately controlled evidence, and restore only after the boundary repair is validated.

questions.title: Transparency that changes user behavior
questions.stem: An educational adviser drafts scholarship suggestions. Students assume the list is exhaustive and sometimes miss deadlines for programs absent from the indexed dataset. The service cannot guarantee complete coverage, and advisers can help investigate unusual circumstances. Which design BEST makes the limitation actionable while maintaining the usefulness of the recommendations?

options.text: Hide all suggestions with uncertain eligibility and present the remaining list as complete because every visible item has strong evidence.
options.why: Confidence in listed items does not establish coverage completeness.

options.text: Show source coverage and freshness, explain that suggestions are non-exhaustive, and offer an adviser escalation path for missing or uncertain eligibility situations.
options.why: It gives users relevant limits and a concrete alternative.

options.text: Require students to accept broad liability terms before viewing results and keep recommendation coverage and dataset age undisclosed.
options.why: Liability wording does not enable an informed user decision.

options.text: Add a generic AI disclaimer in the footer while labeling the recommendation list as the definitive set of scholarships available.
options.why: The main claim still encourages the harmful interpretation.

questions.decision: Transparency should expose the limitation relevant to the user's decision and provide a usable route when it matters.

questions.title: Discovery of the missing authority
questions.stem: An executive asks for an AI assistant that closes overdue customer complaints. A demonstration can draft persuasive replies, but support, legal and account managers disagree on what counts as closure and whether compensation is allowed. The team is ready to choose an orchestration library. What should the architect do FIRST to reduce the largest project uncertainty?

options.text: Observe representative complaints and agree closure criteria, authorized actions, exception owners and baselines with the responsible stakeholders.
options.why: This establishes the unresolved outcome and authority before scope selection.

options.text: Map the demonstration's reply-writing steps into an architecture and ask legal to approve that design before interviewing support and account managers.
options.why: The prototype does not establish the other stakeholders' closure requirements.

options.text: Interview executives about desired turnaround and document a time-saving baseline, leaving compensation and closure definitions to the implementation team.
options.why: It gathers value information but leaves the main authority conflict unresolved.

options.text: Run a workshop comparing orchestration libraries with all departments, using their preferred framework as the common definition of the closure process.
options.why: Agreement on tooling cannot replace agreement on business authority.

questions.decision: Resolve decision rights and success criteria during discovery; architecture selection cannot arbitrate them implicitly.

questions.title: Communicating a measured compromise
questions.stem: A product sponsor wants a cheaper, faster model. Engineers show it passes routine tests but misses critical multilingual cases; the current model meets the quality gate and stays within budget. The sponsor is willing to consider narrower scope. Which TWO communication elements BEST support an informed decision rather than a technical veto or an unsupported promise?

options.text: Offer bounded alternatives such as validated routing or narrower language scope, with owners and evidence needed before changing the current release commitment.
options.why: It makes feasible options and verification obligations explicit.

options.text: Describe all cheaper models as categorically unsuitable and decline to compare any narrower scope or routed operating option.
options.why: That obscures feasible constrained alternatives.

options.text: Promise that a stronger system prompt will fix the multilingual misses after rollout so the sponsor can announce immediate savings.
options.why: The repair and savings are not validated.

options.text: Present measured results by important workload slice, explaining which proposed benefit conflicts with the non-negotiable critical-case requirement.
options.why: This connects evidence to the actual decision constraint.

options.text: Present only the cheaper model's published benchmark and token price because product leadership should decide implementation details independently.
options.why: Those inputs omit the workload's known failure.

questions.decision: Communicate measured trade-offs in terms of commitments and choices, separating proven options from hypotheses requiring validation.

questions.title: A usable service commitment
questions.stem: A payroll assistant answers policy questions quickly but sometimes cannot access a required regional source. Sales promises all questions resolved in two seconds; operations measures first token and excludes source outages. Payroll officers need supported answers or a timely explicit handoff. Which revised commitment BEST aligns user expectations, measurement and operational responsibility before a wider customer launch?

options.text: Exclude every question requiring regional data from service measurement while continuing to market regional payroll coverage to all customers.
options.why: The exclusions contradict the advertised capability.

options.text: Promise best-effort accuracy without any response target, leaving regional-source failures to individual support staff to resolve informally.
options.why: That lacks a usable service commitment and owner.

options.text: Keep the universal resolution promise and report first-token latency because a visible response starts the user's support experience.
options.why: First token is not supported resolution or handoff.

options.text: Agree a measurable supported-answer-or-handoff completion target with defined traffic, dependency treatment and escalation ownership, and validate it on representative workload.
options.why: It defines the delivered outcome and how exceptions are handled.

questions.decision: Define what completion means and who handles exceptions; an SLA must describe the service users actually receive.

questions.title: A documented handoff fails its recovery rehearsal
questions.stem: A service has complete runbooks, named owners and approved deployment access. During the receiving team's recovery rehearsal, restoring the RAG index fails because the recovery role cannot decrypt the backup. Normal serving is unaffected. Production acceptance requires recovery within two hours, and the current role was intended to perform this operation. Which TWO actions BEST close the demonstrated handoff gap?

options.text: Add another architecture diagram and accept the handoff because normal serving passed all model-quality tests.
options.why: The demonstrated recovery failure remains unaddressed.

options.text: Repeat the receiving team's recovery exercise and record the end-to-end result against the two-hour objective before accepting readiness.
options.why: Documentation alone does not prove the repaired recovery works.

options.text: Replace the named recovery owner with the developer's unrestricted account and skip the repeat rehearsal to preserve the handoff date.
options.why: This avoids neither privilege risk nor unverified recovery.

options.text: Correct the recovery role's narrowly required backup-decryption access through the approved access process, without broadening unrelated production privileges.
options.why: This repairs the specific missing capability.

options.text: Relax the recovery target after the failure without an explicit service-owner decision, treating the original commitment as an aspirational guideline.
options.why: The existing acceptance requirement cannot change implicitly.

questions.decision: Handoff evidence includes exercised capability; repair the failed control and demonstrate the receiver can meet the agreed recovery objective.

questions.title: Feedback whose provenance changed
questions.stem: A call-center dashboard suddenly reports twice as many negative assistant ratings. Investigation shows the rating button was moved to the escalation screen; users who resolved cases normally rarely see it. The prompt, model and case mix are unchanged. Supervisors propose an urgent prompt rewrite based on the new aggregate. Which response BEST establishes what the feedback actually supports before selecting a behavioral change?

options.text: Audit the feedback collection denominator and exposure change, compare like-for-like case slices and inspect rated outcomes before attributing the shift to assistant behavior.
options.why: The sampling mechanism changed while the system did not.

options.text: Discard every new rating permanently because a changed interface makes all individual complaints invalid regardless of their case evidence.
options.why: Individual failures may still be real and useful.

options.text: Average old and new raw rating totals to smooth the apparent regression, retaining the same mixed exposure denominator in future reports.
options.why: Smoothing does not repair measurement comparability.

options.text: Rewrite the prompt immediately because a higher negative-rating count directly establishes a decline in all users' answer quality.
options.why: The count is confounded by collection exposure.

questions.decision: Treat feedback collection as part of the evidence pipeline; a changed sampling interface can mimic a product regression.

questions.title: A pilot question before a procurement answer
questions.stem: A retail group wants AI support in stores with unstable connectivity. Headquarters demonstrates a cloud-only assistant on fast office Wi-Fi, and managers request a fleet rollout. Store staff need access during stockroom shifts, but the project has not measured connectivity or identified which tasks can tolerate delayed responses. Which next step BEST resolves the earliest lifecycle gap?

options.text: Declare the demonstration a successful pilot and transfer connectivity troubleshooting to store managers during rollout.
options.why: The demonstration does not represent the intended environment.

options.text: Purchase the largest cloud-model quota immediately so infrastructure capacity cannot delay responses once stores begin using the assistant.
options.why: Quota cannot remedy disconnected operating conditions.

options.text: Observe representative store workflows and connectivity, separate time-critical from deferrable tasks, and agree fallback expectations before validating a deployment design.
options.why: This establishes actual operating requirements before rollout design.

options.text: Require every store to stop time-critical tasks during outages without discussing the operational impact with local stakeholders.
options.why: That imposes an unvalidated business requirement.

questions.decision: Discovery must cover the real operating environment; a favorable demonstration is not evidence that requirements have been established.

questions.title: A design decision ready for implementation
questions.stem: A bank chooses a constrained workflow instead of a free-running agent for dispute handling. A delivery partner joins after the decision and needs to implement it across two systems. The choice depends on approval boundaries, transaction idempotency and a future review trigger. Which THREE artifacts most directly carry the design rationale into implementation without forcing the partner to rediscover the original constraints?

options.text: Acceptance scenarios and operational guidance demonstrating normal, uncertain-outcome and escalation paths with named receiving responsibilities.
options.why: This makes behavior and operational expectations verifiable.

options.text: Versioned interface and state-transition contracts specifying operation identity, authorization checks, failure handling and ownership at each boundary.
options.why: This translates the decision into implementable contracts.

options.text: A collection of prototype screenshots and the chosen framework's marketing overview, leaving transaction semantics to implementation preference.
options.why: These do not define the important system invariants.

options.text: An architecture decision record comparing feasible alternatives, linking the chosen workflow to approval and reliability requirements and its reconsideration conditions.
options.why: This preserves why the choice was made and when it may change.

options.text: A transcript of every design meeting without a maintained decision summary, relying on the partner to infer the final accepted option.
options.why: Raw discussion does not establish a clear implementable decision.

questions.decision: Implementation guidance needs rationale, contracts and verifiable operating behavior, not merely a diagram or historical conversation.

questions.title: Monitoring evidence reopens design assumptions
questions.stem: A deployed assistant meets its original English-language support targets. A merger introduces a new customer population with different document formats and legal obligations. Executives want the team to treat this as routine prompt maintenance because the architecture already passed review. Which lifecycle response BEST reflects the material change while keeping existing service stable?

options.text: Reuse the original acceptance result and add new-language examples directly to production because the existing architecture is already approved.
options.why: Prior evidence does not cover new requirements or populations.

options.text: Stop all existing users immediately and rebuild the entire system before investigating whether the new population needs different controls.
options.why: The change does not automatically invalidate the proven existing path.

options.text: Revisit discovery and risk assumptions for the new population, update acceptance evidence and scope, and stage validated changes while retaining the proven existing path.
options.why: Material changes can reopen earlier lifecycle decisions.

options.text: Measure only global satisfaction after onboarding the merged population and revisit the architecture if that average declines materially.
options.why: A global average can mask new population-specific obligations.

questions.decision: Lifecycle phases are revisited when assumptions change; retain validated service while assessing the new scope explicitly.

questions.title: Approved scope, unaccepted operating ownership
questions.stem: A read-only research assistant's expansion to filing submission has already passed discovery, authority review, design approval and representative acceptance tests. Release configuration is ready, but no receiving team has accepted alert response, filing correction or credential-rotation responsibility. The sponsor says the remaining gap is just another design discussion. Which TWO actions BEST complete the actual unfinished lifecycle work?

options.text: Remove filing alerts temporarily so the lack of an incident owner cannot generate unhandled notifications during launch week.
options.why: Suppressing signals does not complete handoff.

options.text: Exercise the correction, alert and credential procedures with that owner, recording acceptance or remaining limitations against the agreed operating requirements.
options.why: This demonstrates the owner can fulfill the transferred responsibilities.

options.text: Restart model selection and repeat already-passed research-summary tests, treating every release delay as insufficient design validation.
options.why: The supplied evidence locates a different unfinished phase.

options.text: Release without an owner because successful acceptance tests make later alerts and correction responsibilities self-evident to every team.
options.why: Technical acceptance does not assign operating responsibility.

options.text: Secure explicit acceptance of the filing service's operational and incident responsibilities from a capable receiving owner before production release.
options.why: The missing element is accountable operations ownership.

questions.decision: Identify the unfinished phase from evidence; approved scope and working implementation still need accepted operational ownership.

questions.title: Managed policy versus a local convenience rule
questions.stem: A team already excludes production credentials and centrally manages a deny rule for an unapproved network destination. A developer adds a repository-local allow rule for the same destination to unblock a debugging command. The command remains denied, and the managed rule is intentional. The approved environment offers a sanitized diagnostic mirror. Which response BEST follows the permissions hierarchy and preserves useful debugging?

options.text: Remove the central deny configuration from the developer's checkout so the local allow rule becomes the only relevant policy.
options.why: The developer cannot unilaterally remove the organizational boundary.

options.text: Use the approved diagnostic mirror and explain the managed restriction; request policy-owner review only if the permitted evidence proves insufficient.
options.why: A local rule cannot supersede an intentional managed restriction.

options.text: Repeat the local allow rule in CLAUDE.md and assume a more prominent instruction can override the execution-policy decision.
options.why: Guidance does not override managed enforcement.

options.text: Declare debugging impossible without trying the approved mirror because every denied destination implies the whole diagnostic task is prohibited.
options.why: The permitted alternative may satisfy the actual task.

questions.decision: Read the effective permission boundary and use an authorized diagnostic path; do not treat denial as a prompt-strength problem.

questions.title: AI assistance with review capacity
questions.stem: A development team uses AI to generate larger pull requests, increasing code volume but slowing review and raising rollback frequency. Reviewers report difficulty checking unfamiliar cross-module changes. Existing CI catches unit failures but not all integration behavior. Management wants higher delivered throughput rather than more generated lines. Which TWO workflow changes BEST target the observed bottleneck?

options.text: Use AI for bounded changes with explicit acceptance criteria and smaller reviewable increments, measuring lead time and rework rather than generated volume.
options.why: This aligns assistance with review and delivery capacity.

options.text: Require relevant integration verification and human review of consequential boundaries, using AI to prepare evidence and investigate failures before submission.
options.why: It strengthens the checks associated with observed regressions.

options.text: Automatically merge larger AI-generated pull requests after unit tests so human reviewers stop limiting the generation pipeline's throughput.
options.why: This removes review while integration risk remains unresolved.

options.text: Set a target for generated lines per developer and compare teams on that metric before revising the release workflow.
options.why: Generated volume is not delivered useful throughput.

options.text: Give the model the entire repository on every edit and increase request size without changing review or integration practices.
options.why: More context does not solve the demonstrated review bottleneck.

questions.decision: Optimize the complete delivery workflow; generation speed is useful only when changes can be verified, reviewed and operated.

questions.title: A tool result that reports failure
questions.stem: A coding assistant invokes a project generator. The HTTP request succeeds, but the returned tool result contains an application error indicating the output directory was unwritable. The agent reports that the project was created because it checked only transport status. Which change BEST prevents this operational false success without treating all valid HTTP responses as failures? An older output directory from a previous run may already exist.

options.text: Check that an output directory exists and report success, without distinguishing artifacts from previous runs or reading the application result.
options.why: The existing directory may be stale and the current run failed.

options.text: Validate the structured application result and the expected newly produced artifact, then address the reported permission failure before retrying.
options.why: Both execution status and the fresh requested outcome need verification.

options.text: Retry a fixed number of times before inspecting the error, assuming any filesystem problem is transient if transport succeeded.
options.why: The reported unwritable directory calls for targeted remediation first.

options.text: Trust HTTP success but schedule a later artifact check, reporting project creation as complete while the check remains pending.
options.why: The available application error already contradicts completion.

questions.decision: Check success at the user's requested outcome boundary, using the structured tool result and observable artifact.

questions.title: A pinned dependency with the wrong architecture
questions.stem: A team documents and pins its formatter dependency, and a setup check confirms the correct package version is installed. On fresh ARM machines the command fails before reading any project file with an executable-format error; the same pinned version works on x86 machines. The release package contains architecture-specific binaries. Which TWO actions BEST target the environment failure without disabling formatting validation?

options.text: Suppress the formatter error and treat the setup version check as proof that formatting validation completed successfully.
options.why: Installed version does not establish executable compatibility or task success.

options.text: Select or build the supported ARM artifact through the established setup mechanism and verify fresh-machine setup on the affected platform.
options.why: This repairs and checks the actual platform dependency.

options.text: Inspect the selected binary architecture and package-resolution path, reproducing the failure with the formatter's version command outside the repository workload.
options.why: This isolates executable compatibility from project formatting.

options.text: Change source-file formatting rules and add prompt examples, assuming the executable error arises from unsupported code style in the repository.
options.why: The process fails before reading source files.

options.text: Unpin all formatter versions and let each developer install whichever package first succeeds, omitting shared platform checks.
options.why: This replaces a diagnosable compatibility issue with uncontrolled variation.

questions.decision: A pinned dependency can still select an incompatible platform artifact; localize startup failure before changing the task or validation policy.

drills.title: Cache and retrieval release review
drills.stem: Judge each proposal independently against the stated obligation. Choose Yes or No in every row; no fixed number of Yes answers is implied.

rows.text: Requirement: immediate permission revocation. Proposal: recheck current access before returning cached answers, rejecting artifacts whose access cannot be verified.
rows.why: Current enforcement avoids relying solely on stale cached permission metadata.

rows.text: Requirement: trace changing policy. Proposal: record only the model version, because the retrieval source is maintained by another team.
rows.why: Source and configuration versions affect reproducibility.

rows.text: Requirement: exact catalog lookup. Proposal: evaluate a lexical identifier path alongside dense retrieval on identifier-specific held-out cases.
rows.why: The experiment targets the query shape without assuming an unmeasured improvement.

rows.text: Requirement: tenant isolation. Proposal: share answers keyed by question text alone whenever prompts look similar across tenants.
rows.why: Question equality does not establish identical authorization or policy.

rows.text: Requirement: reduce prefix cost. Proposal: verify actual write/read usage and compute weighted cost including cache misses.
rows.why: Realized cache economics require both modes and workload usage.

drills.title: Operational ownership review
drills.stem: For each row, decide whether the proposed evidence satisfies the particular obligation. Judge rows independently.

rows.text: Obligation: transfer operations ownership. Evidence: receiving team rehearses deployment and rollback using approved access and accepts incident responsibilities.
rows.why: Practical capability and accepted responsibility support the transfer.

rows.text: Obligation: prove filing readiness. Evidence: read-only research summaries passed their original accuracy test.
rows.why: A different consequential capability needs its own acceptance evidence.

rows.text: Obligation: fair shortlist exposure. Evidence: overall hiring accuracy improves, while a qualified subgroup is still systematically hidden from reviewers.
rows.why: The aggregate improvement does not address the observed exclusion.

rows.text: Obligation: contain confirmed cache leakage. Proposal: disable the affected cache path and serve verified authorized retrieval while investigating.
rows.why: Containment removes the demonstrated path and preserves a safer fallback.

rows.text: Obligation: preserve approved action parameters. Proposal: an old shipment approval remains valid after the route exceeds the approved transit limit.
rows.why: The materially changed action requires renewed authorization.

drills.title: Choose the next lifecycle intervention
drills.stem: Choose the BEST primary intervention for each situation. Options may repeat. These labels organize this practice exercise and are not an official exam item-format guarantee.

rows.text: Departments disagree on what complaint closure means before any solution scope is accepted.
rows.why: Success and decision authority must be resolved before implementation.

rows.text: A chosen workflow needs tested idempotency contracts and approval-boundary acceptance scenarios before construction proceeds.
rows.why: This checks whether the architecture implements established requirements.

rows.text: Operations must rehearse rollback and accept named incident responsibilities for a quality-tested implementation.
rows.why: The receiving team is establishing operational capability and ownership.

rows.text: A production language regression needs containment, diagnosis and a versioned regression-tested repair.
rows.why: The evidence arises during operation and drives controlled improvement.

rows.text: A proposed new filing capability introduces unresolved legal authority beyond the accepted read-only assistant.
rows.why: The expansion first needs its permitted scope and authority established.
